sentence: Ibuprofen is a painkiller that also treats inflammation.
note: Page title: 'Ibuprofen for adults: painkiller that also treats inflammation - NHS'.

sentence: Inflammation is the swelling and soreness that can come with an injury or a joint problem.
note: Plain definition of a common term.

sentence: It belongs to a group of medicines called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs.
note: Summary of the NHS common-questions page: ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug.

sentence: Ibuprofen comes as tablets, capsules, granules and liquid that are swallowed, and as products that are applied to the skin.
note: Summary named tablets, capsules, granules, liquid and skin products.

sentence: The NHS says it does not usually work well for nerve pain.
note: Summary: ibuprofen doesn't usually work well for nerve pain.

sentence: If ibuprofen does not help, the NHS lists paracetamol, aspirin and co-codamol as other everyday painkillers.
note: Summary listed paracetamol, aspirin and co-codamol as other everyday options.

sentence: According to the NHS, most adults and older teenagers can take ibuprofen, but its page on who can and cannot take it lists several reasons it may not suit someone.
note: Summary: most adults and young people aged 17 and over can take it; NHS lists several reasons not to.

sentence: The NHS says ibuprofen works by lowering the amount of certain hormones in the body that cause pain and swelling.
note: Summary: it acts by lowering hormones that drive pain and swelling.

sentence: With less of these chemicals, there is less pain and less swelling.
note: Follows from the same statement.

sentence: The chemicals involved are called prostaglandins, and the body makes them with the help of enzymes called cyclo-oxygenase.
note: Standard pharmacology; the returned text did not name them.

sentence: The NHS says swallowed forms usually start to ease pain fairly soon, while skin products take a day or two to work.
note: Summary gave about 20 to 30 minutes for swallowed forms and 1 to 2 days for skin products; numbers left out.

sentence: It also says anyone who still needs ibuprofen after several days should check with a doctor.
note: Summary gave a limit of 10 days for adults; number left out.

sentence: The NHS says some people take ibuprofen for many years when a doctor prescribes it.
note: Summary: long-term use is possible for many years if prescribed.

sentence: Ulcers are a risk with long-term use or large amounts, and a doctor may prescribe a stomach-protecting medicine for people at risk.
note: Summary: ulcers a risk with long-term or high-dose use; doctor may prescribe a stomach-protecting medicine.

sentence: The NHS lists indigestion and stomach aches, feeling sick, headaches, a rash, dizziness, and diarrhoea or constipation among the common side effects.
note: Summary of the side-effects page listed these.

sentence: The NHS says ibuprofen can cause dizziness, and it advises against driving or cycling until the feeling passes.
note: Summary: ibuprofen can cause dizziness; avoid driving or cycling until you feel better.

sentence: Gels and other skin products cause fewer side effects than swallowed forms, because less of the medicine gets into the body.
note: Summary stated this for topical gels without a citation. The returned summary blended several pages, so the page is named as the likely source.

sentence: Rarer serious effects include stomach ulcers or bleeding in the stomach, a serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis, and kidney problems.
note: Summary of the NHS side-effects page.

sentence: The NHS says black or bloody poo, swollen ankles, or changes in urination are reasons to contact NHS 111 or a doctor.
note: Summary: call 111 or a doctor for black or bloody stools, ankle swelling or urination changes.

sentence: A swollen throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, needs a call to 999.
note: Summary: call 999 for swollen throat or tongue or difficulty breathing.

sentence: MedlinePlus, a US source, says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen may raise the risk of a heart attack or stroke, and that the risk is higher with long-term or high-amount use.
note: Summary: MedlinePlus warns of higher heart attack or stroke risk, higher with long-term or high-dose use.

sentence: The NHS says taking ibuprofen with a meal or with milk makes an upset stomach less likely.
note: Both summaries: take with food or milk; less likely to upset the stomach.

sentence: On alcohol, the NHS says a small amount is usually not a problem, but heavy drinking can irritate the stomach.
note: Summary: moderate alcohol usually acceptable; heavy drinking can irritate the stomach.

sentence: MedlinePlus says heavy drinking is one of the things that raises the risk of stomach bleeding with NSAIDs.
note: Summary: risk of ulcers and bleeding rises with older age, poor health, smoking or heavy drinking.

sentence: Some UK patient leaflets go further and tell people not to drink alcohol, because it may add to side effects in the stomach, gut or nervous system.
note: Summary said UK leaflets advise against alcohol. The returned summary blended several pages, so the page is named as the likely source.

sentence: Sources advise checking with a doctor or pharmacist before combining ibuprofen with other NSAIDs, including aspirin.
note: Summary: check with a clinician before combining with other NSAIDs including aspirin; the review is the likely source. The returned summary blended several pages, so the page is named as the likely source.

sentence: Medicines that can interact include diuretics and ACE inhibitors, which add to the risk of kidney harm, anticoagulants such as warfarin, which add to bleeding risk, and lithium.
note: Summary gave these examples. The returned summary blended several pages, so the page is named as the likely source.

sentence: The NHS lists reasons not to take ibuprofen, including a past allergic reaction to aspirin or another NSAID, pregnancy, a history of stomach bleeding or ulcers, and severe heart, kidney or liver failure.
note: Summary of the NHS who-can-and-cannot page.

sentence: It says people over 65 are more likely to get stomach ulcers with ibuprofen.
note: Summary: if you're over 65, ibuprofen can make you more likely to get stomach ulcers.

sentence: Asthma, hay fever and allergies are listed as conditions to discuss with a doctor first.
note: Summary of NHS page.

sentence: Heart disease, mild to moderate heart failure and uncontrolled high blood pressure are also listed as reasons for caution.
note: Summary of NHS page.

sentence: MedlinePlus says people who have recently had a heart attack should not take ibuprofen unless a doctor directs it.

sentence: UK leaflets also name bleeding disorders and dehydration as reasons to avoid it or to use it only with medical supervision.
